newsitem.title: INDIA: Silver-India prices fall, fresh buying seen.
newsitem.headline: Silver-India prices fall, fresh buying seen.

text.p: Indian silver prices, shadowing global trends, opened sharply lower on Wednesday and may fall further this week, but buying ahead of a Hindu festival could lead a quick recovery, bullion dealers said.
They said silver opened 55 rupees down at 6,920 rupees per kg on the Bombay bullion market.
"I expect prices to fall further," said bullion dealer Bhayabhai Sanghvi. Silver prices have fallen by 175 rupees per kg in the past week.
Dealers said New York spot silver had fallen to an 18-month low of around $4.82 an ounce on Tuesday on heavy short-covering and speculative selling.
Traders in Tokyo said bearish sentiment in silver could pressure other precious metal prices in the near-term.
Gold prices in Bombay opened 15 rupees lower at 5,155 rupees per kg on Wednesday in line with a subdued trend in silver.
Dealers said they expected silver prices to fall to 6,800-6,850 rupees per kg in the next couple of days.
"Traders are not panicky because the market may immediately find fresh festival buying," said Mahavir Jain, a jeweller.
Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which falls this year on November 11, traditionally triggers demand for both gold and silver across India, coinciding with the harvest of winter crops.
"Farmers have been putting more money in gold and silver now than before," Sanghvi said.

In the last two years, Indian money markets have been tight, stock markets dull and the construction industry subdued. But gold and silver have offered a good opportunity to invest as a hedge against inflation and currency fluctuations, he said.
Dealers estimate India's annual requirement of silver at 2,500 tonnes. The amount is entirely imported.
Sanghvi said industrial demand for silver in India had been rising and higher domestic prices provide a margin of at least 2.0 percent over imported silver, making imports attractive.
India, implementing a package of economic reforms, has allowed free imports of gold and silver by Indian expatriates, subject to customs duty.
"The margin is good despite an import duty of 500 rupees per kg of silver," Sanghvi added.
